data.title: User-Execution Lure (Double Extension / Icon Spoof)
data.summary: The sample relies on the victim taking a specific action to launch it — opening an attachment, enabling macros, running a file disguised with a spoofed icon or double extension — rather than exploiting a vulnerability.
data.description:
This is the lowest-cost delivery mechanism available and remains common precisely because
it needs no exploit to work, only a convincing enough lure and a brief lapse in attention:
a file named invoice.pdf.exe with a PDF icon, a document whose content is a fabricated
warning instructing the user to 'enable content' to view it, or an archive whose contents
are named to encourage opening without a second thought.
data.recommendation:
* Configure Explorer and mail clients to always show full file extensions; a double-extension lure depends entirely on this being hidden by default.
* Disable macro execution by default for documents originating from the internet, and require explicit justification to re-enable per document.
* Train users on the specific lure pattern observed (icon spoofing, fabricated 'enable content' prompts) rather than generic phishing awareness alone — concrete examples transfer better than abstractions.
data.short_recommendation: Show full file extensions by default and disable macros for internet-sourced documents; the lure depends on both being hidden.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Named the dropped executable 'Invoice.pdf.exe' with an embedded PDF-viewer icon resource to spoof the file type at a glance.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Dropped file used a spoofed icon resource and double extension to encourage the victim to open it as a document.
